summary: Describes three abstract GSS-API interfaces for encapsulating and decapsulating context tokens and for comparing object identifiers (OIDs), and specifies C bindings for them.

eli5.summary: Security programs often wrap and unwrap special packages and need to check whether two labels are the same. This defines three small helper functions for doing those jobs.

questions: how to compare oids in gss-api
subtitle: Three small GSS-API functions for adding and removing the standard token header and for comparing OIDs.

tldr.problem: Protocols such as SASL GS2 need to add and remove the mechanism-independent header on GSS-API context tokens, and applications need to compare mechanism OIDs, but GSS-API had no calls for this.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6339 defines GSS_Encapsulate_token, GSS_Decapsulate_token and GSS_OID_equal, with C bindings and a test vector.
tldr.outcome: GSS-API libraries can offer these operations in a standard way. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 6339 is a Proposed Standard. The unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why These Calls Exist
sections.content:
The Generic Security Service API (GSS-API, RFC 2743) provides security services to applications through a variety of authentication mechanisms. RFC 2744 gives widely implemented C bindings.

For initial context tokens, a mechanism-independent token format may be used. Some protocols, for example SASL GS2 (RFC 5801), need to add and remove this token header. It contains some ASN.1 tags, a length and the mechanism OID. RFC 6339 adds two interfaces for this, and a third for comparing OIDs, which is useful for validating that a negotiated mechanism matches the requested one.

Sections 3, 4, 5, 6 and 8 are to be treated as code components, so the text can be reused as implementation documentation.
sections.eli5: Sometimes a program has to put a standard label on a security message or take it off, and check whether two labels match. These new helpers do that.

sections.title: Encapsulating a Token
sections.content:
GSS_Encapsulate_token adds the mechanism-independent token header to GSS-API context token data. Its inputs are input_token, the token data to encapsulate, and token_oid, the object identifier of the mechanism. The output is output_token, which the caller must release with GSS_Release_buffer().

It returns GSS_S_COMPLETE on success or GSS_S_FAILURE if encapsulation failed for reasons unspecified at the GSS-API level. The C binding is gss_encapsulate_token, taking a gss_const_buffer_t, a gss_const_OID and a gss_buffer_t for the output.
sections.eli5: This puts the standard label on a message, saying which security method it belongs to.

sections.title: Decapsulating a Token
sections.content:
GSS_Decapsulate_token removes the mechanism-independent token header from an initial GSS-API context token. The inputs are the token to decapsulate and the expected object identifier of the token. The output is the decapsulated token data, released with GSS_Release_buffer().

Besides GSS_S_COMPLETE and GSS_S_FAILURE, it can return GSS_S_DEFECTIVE_TOKEN, which means the token failed consistency checks, for example an OID mismatch or ASN.1 DER length errors. The C binding is gss_decapsulate_token.
sections.eli5: This takes the label off and checks it is the one you expected. If the label looks wrong, it says the message is defective.

sections.title: Comparing OIDs
sections.content:
GSS_OID_equal compares two object identifiers for equality. It returns non-zero when neither OID is GSS_C_NO_OID and the two are equal, and 0 when they are not identical or either is GSS_C_NO_OID.

The value GSS_C_NO_OID never matches any OID, including GSS_C_NO_OID itself. The C binding is gss_oid_equal, which takes two gss_const_OID values.
sections.eli5: This asks whether two name tags are the same. An empty tag never matches anything, not even another empty tag.

sections.title: Test Vector
sections.content: For encapsulation, if the input token is the 3-byte sequence foo and the OID is 1.2.840.113554.1.2.2, which encodes to the 9-byte sequence \x2a\x86\x48\x86\xf7\x12\x01\x02\x02, the output should be the 16-byte sequence \x60\x0e\x06\x09\x2a\x86\x48\x86\xf7\x12\x01\x02\x02\x66\x6f\x6f. The same values can test the decapsulation interface.
sections.eli5: The RFC gives one worked example so builders can check their code gives the same answer.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 2743 and RFC 2744 are inherited. Encapsulation of data does not provide any kind of integrity or confidentiality.

Implementations need to treat input as potentially untrustworthy when dereferencing memory objects, to avoid security vulnerabilities. ASN.1 DER length fields are called out as a common source of mistakes.
sections.eli5: Putting a label on a message does not lock it. Also, never trust a label's size without checking it.

data.title: GSS_Encapsulate_token test vector
data.code:
input_token: "foo" (3 bytes)
token_oid:   1.2.840.113554.1.2.2
             "\x2a\x86\x48\x86\xf7\x12\x01\x02\x02" (9 bytes)
output:      "\x60\x0e\x06\x09\x2a\x86\x48\x86\xf7\x12\x01\x02\x02\x66\x6f\x6f" (16 bytes)
